A green that has to read well in a listing photo, not just roll true

A backyard putting green in Four Corners costs about $14–$30 a square foot installed, typically $18–$25, as of September 2026. On a lot run as a short-term rental, the green is as much a marketing photo as a golf feature, which changes what contour, fringe and placement need to accomplish.

Reviewed by Luis Austin, owner · Last reviewed September 21, 2026

What the best putting-green installer near you does differently for a listing

What the best putting-green installer near you in Four Corners does differently on a rental property comes down to two things: contour and fringe that photograph well from the patio slider, and cups placed where they show up in a wide shot rather than tucked in a corner. A flat, technically sound green can still look unremarkable in a listing photo if the fringe transition is a straight line instead of a soft curve, and on a property competing with dozens of similar rentals for a booking, that photo does real work.

Golf-adjacent lots and what the HOA wants to see

A number of Four Corners subdivisions were built around or near a golf course, and lots backing onto a fairway often carry design-review language about anything visible from that side of the property, greens included. A submission that shows the green's footprint, height and color, plus how it reads from the course side rather than just the street side, tends to move through review faster in these communities than a bare site plan.

Why a contoured green still needs an overall slope

Even with tiers and breaks built into the surface for play, a Four Corners putting green's base still carries the same one to two percent overall grade toward a drainage point that any lawn does, so the two jobs, holding a shape and shedding water, happen at once rather than one after the other. A green shaped purely for interesting breaks without that underlying slope will hold water in its lowest tier after every storm, regardless of how well the ball rolls the rest of the time. Getting both requirements satisfied in the same base is what separates a green built by someone experienced with the shaping from a flat pad with decoration on top.

Seaming the putting surface and fringe as separate pieces

The short putting surface and the taller fringe turf around a Four Corners green get cut and seamed as two distinct pieces rather than one continuous roll, since they're different products at different pile heights doing different jobs. That seam is placed deliberately along the design's edge line so it reads as a mowing transition once grooming is finished, not as a visible patch where two products meet. Getting this seam line right the first time matters more on a green than on a lawn, since the edge is exactly where a chip shot lands and a rough transition is the most visible spot on the entire surface.

Say you have a 420 sq ft green and fringe combination

Say a Four Corners rental wants a 420 sq ft putting green with fringe added behind the pool cage, replacing a plain grass strip that never got much use. At the typical $18–$25 range, that prices out to roughly $7,560 to $10,500 installed, covering the contoured green, two cups, fringe turf and edging. Because the lot backs onto a community pond, the state standard's 10-foot waterbody setback factors into how close the contouring can run to the rear property line, which is worth confirming before the layout is finalized rather than after. A property manager listing the home would typically want the green visible from the lanai in exterior photos, so placement gets planned around the camera angle a listing photographer is likely to use as much as around the terrain itself.

Why stimp speed depends on following the maker's numbers, not a house habit

Reaching a specific stimp reading on a Four Corners green depends on matching the fiber manufacturer's own infill rate and grooming instructions for that particular nylon or polyethylene product, rather than applying the same roughly one to two pounds per square foot habit used across a lawn. Two installers using the same fiber but different infill weights or grooming patterns can hand off greens that stimp noticeably differently even though both look identical on delivery day. Asking which manufacturer's numbers a green was built to, and confirming infill was measured rather than eyeballed, is the more reliable way to predict how it will actually play.

Contour built for a rotating set of guests, not one golfer's habits

A green built for one household's owner can be shaped around that person's preferred shots; a rental-property green gets used by guests with a wide range of skill levels, most of them casual, over a single weekend. A gentler break and a slightly larger cup radius hold up better across that kind of turnover than a green designed for a single serious golfer's practice routine, and the fringe still needs the same true-roll backing and pile height regardless of who's using it that week.

What a green retrofit risks hitting underground

Cutting out an established Four Corners lawn to make room for a green's deeper four- to six-inch excavation risks striking an old irrigation line that was capped at the valve when the original lawn went in, since a line that no longer waters anything doesn't always get marked or remembered years later. Confirming where any capped zones ran before digging avoids severing a line that, while inactive, may still be tied into the broader irrigation system serving the rest of the property. A quick check with whoever handled the original lawn conversion, or a look at the valve box layout, settles this before the first shovel of a retrofit goes in.

Grooming more often in the dry months, differently in the wet ones

A Four Corners green needs more frequent light grooming through the dry season, since dust and pollen build up without rain to clear them and a consistent roll depends on keeping the surface free of both. Once June through September rainy season sets in, storms handle some of that clearing on their own, but grooming right after a storm rather than days later matters more here than in the dry months, since damp infill settles differently under a brush than dry infill does. Matching the routine's frequency and timing to the season keeps stimp speed more consistent across the whole year instead of drifting between wet and dry stretches.

Questions people ask

Does a putting green need HOA approval on a Four Corners golf-course lot?

Most golf-adjacent communities require design review for anything visible from the course or the street, greens included. A submission with the footprint, height and color usually covers what the board asks for.

Is a smaller green worth it just for listing photos?

Often yes. A modest green with clean contour and fringe photographs better than a larger one with a plain rectangular edge, and it costs less to install and maintain.
